## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="m2-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Unit commitment</dt><dd>Which plants are on in each hour, decided together with how much each makes: on/off switches, start-up and no-load costs, minimum outputs and run times.</dd>
<dt>LP relaxation</dt><dd>The same model with every switch allowed between 0 and 1. Its cost, $168,975, is a lower bound; its schedule, a peaker 5% on, cannot be operated.</dd>
<dt>Branch and bound</dt><dd>Split a fractional switch into off and on, solve both, and prune any node whose bound cannot beat the best plan. Five branchings proved $173,200.</dd>
<dt>No shadow prices</dt><dd>The mixed-integer solve returns no duals, and its cost jumps: at 23:00 each of the first 5 MWh costs $40, the 6th $2,140.</dd>
<dt>Conditional prices</dt><dd>Fix the switches and re-solve the LP: $40, and $100 from 19:00 to 21:00, valid for this commitment only.</dd>
<dt>Uplift</dt><dd>At those prices the peaker is $9,200 short of its costs: start-up, no-load and hours at its minimum. Markets pay such gaps outside the price.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>How the bound climbs, and why formulations matter</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

The tree on this page branched only on the peaker's switches. Each branching fixed one switch "on" and raised the best bound:

| Node | Fixed so far | Bound |
|---|---|---|
| Root | nothing | \$168,975 |
| 2 | on at 19:00 | \$169,510 |
| 4 | and 21:00 | \$169,735 |
| 6 | and 18:00 | \$170,575 |
| 8 | and 22:00 | \$171,415 |
| 10 | and 17:00: every switch whole | \$173,200 |

The root gap was \$4,225, or 2.4% of the best plan. A tighter formulation (other ways to write minimum run times, start-ups and ramps) gives a relaxation closer to the whole-number optimum, and a smaller tree; [Knueven, Ostrowski and Watson (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1287/ijoc.2019.0944) compare many.

HiGHS adds presolve, cutting planes and heuristics to the same search. By default it stops once the gap is below 0.01% (`mip_rel_gap = 0.0001`, [HiGHS options](https://ergo-code.github.io/HiGHS/dev/options/definitions/)); here it reached 0%.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Prices when plants switch on and off</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

A dual is the slope of the best cost as one right-hand side changes. With switches, the best cost jumps where a switch flips:

| MWh added at 23:00 | 1 to 5 | 6 | 7 to 10 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Each MWh costs | \$40 | \$2,140 | \$40 |

The 6th MWh keeps the peaker on: \$300 no-load plus 30 MWh at \$100, less 29 MWh of combined-cycle output at \$40, compared with 5 MWh added.

Fixing the switches and reading the LP's duals is the starting point of [O'Neill, Sotkiewicz, Hobbs, Rothkopf and Stewart (2005)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejor.2003.12.011), who also price the fixed decisions themselves. FERC describes uplift payments as "the portion of the cost of reliably serving load that is not included in market prices" ([Order No. 844](https://www.ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2020-06/Order-844.pdf), P 7, 2018).

| The peaker at conditional prices | \$ for the day |
|---|---|
| Paid: 90 MWh at \$40, 180 MWh at \$100 | \$21,600 |
| Running cost: 270 MWh at \$100 | \$27,000 |
| No-load: 6 hours at \$300 | \$1,800 |
| One start | \$2,000 |
| Short: the uplift | \$9,200 |

Other pricing rules have been proposed and used that fold part of these costs into the price, and so move money between plants and loads. Comparing them is a Researcher-tier question.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this model leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>The network: one bus here; M1 put the plants on three buses.</li>
<li>Ramp limits: M1's 40 MW/h rule for the combined-cycle plant is left out (practice question 3 adds it back).</li>
<li>Reserves: operators also commit spare headroom for a plant that trips.</li>
<li>Forecast errors and outages: the day is known in advance here. M8 (upcoming) decides before the uncertainty resolves.</li>
<li>Tomorrow: the day ends with the combined-cycle plant on and treats the night after it as given; real schedules roll forward.</li>
<li>Offers and market rules: costs stand in for offers; real settlements follow each market's tariff.</li>
</ul>
<p>Modeler's note: M5 (upcoming) sizes a microgrid with a mixed-integer program, and the Modeler checkpoint CK-M (upcoming) asks you to formulate, solve and verify a model you have not seen.</p>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="m2-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="duals" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A mixed-integer solver returns shadow prices, just like a linear-program solver.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. HiGHS returned no duals, and the cost has jumps: at 23:00 the 5th MWh costs $40, the 6th $2,140.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="round" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Rounding the relaxation's switches to 0 or 1 gives a workable schedule.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Here rounding keeps the peaker on only at 19:00 and 20:00 and leaves 90 MWh unserved.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="short" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A plant in the cheapest schedule can lose money at the conditional prices.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. The peaker is paid $21,600 against $30,800 of costs; the $9,200 gap needs an uplift payment.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="m2">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="bound" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">A node of the tree has a bound of $171,415. Could some plan below that node cost $170,000?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">Yes, if its switches are whole numbers</li><li data-value="b">No: no plan below a node costs less than its bound</li><li data-value="c">Only if some demand is unserved</li><li data-value="d">It depends on the solver</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>No. Plans below a node only add rules to its relaxation, so none can cost less than $171,415.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="su" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">The peaker's start-up cost doubles to $4,000; its switches stay on from 17:00 to 22:00. The conditional price at 20:00 then…</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">rises by $2,000</li><li data-value="b">rises by $333, a sixth of the extra cost</li><li data-value="c">stays at $100, and the uplift rises by $2,000</li><li data-value="d">falls</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>It stays at $100. With the switches fixed, a start-up cost is a constant: it moves no dual, so the uplift grows to $11,200.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<p>Utilities, and day-ahead market software in regional markets, optimize which units to commit (<a href="https://www.ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2020-06/energy-primer-2020_0.pdf">FERC Energy Primer</a>, p. 37), with many more units, a network and reserves. Uplift payments cover costs the prices miss.</p>
<ul class="m2-links">
<li>Builds on: <a href="m01-dispatch-to-lmp.html">M1</a> (the dispatch LP and its duals), <a href="11-solver.html">lesson 11</a> (a peaker with a minimum output) and <a href="00-grid-operator.html">lesson 0</a> (the plants).</li>
<li>Bridges: <a href="b01-algebra-to-lp.html">B1</a> and <a href="b03-read-check-formulation.html">B3</a>.</li>
<li>Open tools for larger models: <a href="https://docs.pypsa.org/">PyPSA</a>, <a href="https://www.pyomo.org/">Pyomo</a> and <a href="https://jump.dev/">JuMP</a>.</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-sources">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Sources and further reading</p>
<ul>
<li>FERC staff (2020). <a href="https://www.ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2020-06/energy-primer-2020_0.pdf">Energy Primer: A Handbook of Energy Market Basics</a> (PDF), p. 55: day-ahead unit commitment.</li>
<li>FERC (2018). <a href="https://www.ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2020-06/Order-844.pdf">Order No. 844, Uplift Cost Allocation and Transparency in Markets Operated by Regional Transmission Organizations and Independent System Operators</a> (PDF), 163 FERC ¶ 61,041, P 7.</li>
<li>O'Neill, R. P., Sotkiewicz, P. M., Hobbs, B. F., Rothkopf, M. H. and Stewart, W. R. (2005). <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejor.2003.12.011">Efficient market-clearing prices in markets with nonconvexities</a>. European Journal of Operational Research 164(1), 269–285.</li>
<li>Knueven, B., Ostrowski, J. and Watson, J.-P. (2020). <a href="https://doi.org/10.1287/ijoc.2019.0944">On Mixed-Integer Programming Formulations for the Unit Commitment Problem</a>. INFORMS Journal on Computing.</li>
<li>EIA. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/">Hourly Electric Grid Monitor</a> (Form EIA-930): the Southwest Power Pool data behind the day.</li>
<li>HiGHS. <a href="https://ergo-code.github.io/HiGHS/dev/">Documentation</a> of the open-source solver used in the page and, through SciPy, in the notebook.</li>
</ul>
```
